lessonTitle: Aneuploidy and Non-disjunction: Trisomy 21, Turner and Klinefelter Syndromes

blocks.text: A newborn is floppy, has upslanting eyes and a single crease across the palm, and the paediatrician hears a murmur. One extra copy of one small chromosome, present in every cell, explains all of it. How does a single division error in a gamete produce this?

blocks.markdown: **Euploid** cells carry a whole multiple of the haploid number $n = 23$ chromosomes (a normal human somatic cell is diploid, $2n = 46$). **Aneuploidy** means a cell has a chromosome number that is *not* an exact multiple of $n$: one chromosome too many (trisomy, $2n+1 = 47$) or one too few (monosomy, $2n-1 = 45$). Aneuploidy is common at conception and is a major cause of miscarriage. Only a few aneuploidies are compatible with live birth, mainly trisomy 21, trisomy 18, trisomy 13 and sex chromosome aneuploidies, because extra or missing copies of whole chromosomes alter the dosage of hundreds of genes at once. Sex chromosome aneuploidies are better tolerated because of X-inactivation (the extra X chromosomes are silenced except for a few genes) and because the Y chromosome carries few genes.

blocks.title: Non-disjunction
blocks.text: Non-disjunction is the failure of paired chromosomes (homologues in meiosis I) or sister chromatids (in meiosis II or mitosis) to separate and move to opposite poles. The result is daughter cells with an extra chromosome (n+1) and cells missing one (n-1). It is the commonest cause of aneuploidy.

blocks.markdown: **Where the error happens matters.** Recall that in meiosis I the *homologous* chromosomes separate, and in meiosis II the *sister chromatids* separate. If the homologues of chromosome 21 fail to separate in meiosis I, one daughter cell receives both homologues (one from each parent of the gamete-forming person) and the other receives none. Every gamete descended from the affected cell is abnormal. If instead the sister chromatids fail to separate in meiosis II, only the descendants of that one secondary cell are affected, and the other division product is normal. After fertilisation by a normal gamete ($n$), an $n+1$ gamete gives a trisomic zygote ($2n+1 = 47$) and an $n-1$ gamete gives a monosomic zygote (45).

blocks.title: Tracing the gametes of one oocyte with meiosis I non-disjunction of chromosome 21
blocks.prompt: A primary oocyte has non-disjunction of the chromosome 21 pair at meiosis I. Meiosis II is normal. What is the chromosome 21 content of the mature ovum and of the polar bodies, and what happens if the ovum is fertilised by a normal sperm?

steps.text: The primary oocyte contains two chromosome 21 homologues, each made of two sister chromatids (four chromatids in all).

At meiosis I both homologues stay together and move to one pole. The secondary oocyte therefore has either both homologues (2 chromosomes, 4 chromatids) or neither; each outcome is equally likely to be the one kept.

If the secondary oocyte retains both homologues, meiosis II separates the sister chromatids normally, so the ovum has two copies of chromosome 21 (it is disomic for 21, with 24 chromosomes in total). The first polar body has none.
The normal sperm contributes one chromosome 21.
The zygote is 47,XX,+21 or 47,XY,+21 (trisomy 21). If the secondary oocyte had retained neither homologue, fertilisation would produce monosomy 21, which is not viable.

blocks.answer: The ovum carries two copies of chromosome 21; fertilisation by a normal sperm gives trisomy 21 (47 chromosomes). The error arose in maternal meiosis I.

blocks.title: Origin of the extra chromosome 21
blocks.text: About 90-95% of trisomy 21 arises from an error in the maternal gamete, and most maternal errors occur at meiosis I. Most cases (about 95%) are 'free' trisomy 21 from non-disjunction. A small proportion are due to a Robertsonian translocation (covered in a separate unit), and a few percent are mosaic, arising from non-disjunction after fertilisation in an early mitotic division.

blocks.markdown: **Why maternal age matters.** A male makes sperm continuously from puberty, so each sperm has only recently completed meiosis. A female's primary oocytes begin meiosis I in fetal life and then arrest in prophase I (at the diplotene stage) until ovulation, which may be decades later. During this long arrest the proteins that hold the homologues together (such as cohesin) and the chiasmata that link them deteriorate, so with advancing maternal age homologues are more likely to separate incorrectly. The result is a steep, roughly exponential rise in the risk of trisomy, especially after about 35 years. Paternal age has no comparable effect on trisomy 21.

blocks.title: Expected number of affected pregnancies
blocks.prompt: Using the approximate risk in the table above, how many pregnancies with trisomy 21 would you expect among 700 women aged 35, and how does the risk compare with age 30?

steps.text: Risk at 35 is about 1 in 350, which is a probability of 1/350.
Expected cases equals number of women times probability.
Risk at 30 is about 1 in 1000. The ratio of risks is 1000/350, about 2.9.

blocks.answer: About 2 affected pregnancies among 700 women aged 35; the risk is nearly three times the risk at age 30. Note that most babies with Down syndrome are still born to younger women simply because there are many more pregnancies in that group.

rows: Hypotonia, flat facial profile, upslanting palpebral fissures, epicanthic folds, single palmar crease, Brushfield spots, intellectual disability
Atrioventricular septal defect, duodenal atresia, hypothyroidism, increased risk of leukaemia, early-onset Alzheimer disease

blocks.caption: Three common aneuploidies compared.

blocks.markdown: **Sex chromosome aneuploidies.** In Turner syndrome (45,X) the single X is usually maternal and the paternal sex chromosome has been lost, either through non-disjunction in the father or loss in early mitosis. The ovarian follicles degenerate prematurely, so the gonads are replaced by fibrous 'streaks', oestrogen is low and gonadotrophins are high. Most 45,X conceptions miscarry, and a cystic hygroma seen on prenatal ultrasound is a typical clue. In Klinefelter syndrome (47,XXY) the extra X may be of either parental origin. Testicular seminiferous tubules degenerate, producing small firm testes and infertility. Only one X is active in each cell: the others condense into **Barr bodies**, so a 47,XXY male has one Barr body and a 45,X female has none.

items: Euploid = exact multiple of 23; aneuploid = not.
Meiosis I non-disjunction affects all four products; meiosis II non-disjunction affects two of four.
Trisomy 21 is mainly maternal in origin and mainly arises in meiosis I.
Risk rises sharply with maternal age because oocytes remain arrested in prophase I for decades.
Turner = 45,X, no Barr body; Klinefelter = 47,XXY, one Barr body.

blocks.title: Do not confuse the questions
blocks.text: Whether the extra chromosome is of maternal or paternal origin is a separate question from the stage (meiosis I or II) of the error. Say both. Also remember the older age effect applies to maternal age for trisomies; it is not a reason for Turner or Klinefelter syndrome.

points: Non-disjunction is failure of homologues (meiosis I) or sister chromatids (meiosis II/mitosis) to separate, producing n+1 and n-1 cells.
Trisomy 21 (47,+21) causes Down syndrome and is usually maternal in origin and meiosis I; it carries cardiac, duodenal, thyroid and neurodevelopmental features.
Turner (45,X) and Klinefelter (47,XXY) syndromes have recognisable features, summarised in the comparison table.
The risk of trisomy rises steeply with maternal age because oocytes stay arrested in prophase I for decades.

questions.stem: A secondary oocyte fails to separate the sister chromatids of chromosome 18 at meiosis II. Which statement describes the consequence?

options.text: The mature ovum or the polar body derived from that cell has two copies and the other has none
All four products of the original primary oocyte are abnormal
The homologous chromosomes remained together in meiosis I
The error produces polyploidy with 69 chromosomes

questions.correctOptionText: The mature ovum or the polar body derived from that cell has two copies and the other has none

distractorRationale.a: Correct: sister chromatids fail to separate, so one product receives both chromatids (two copies) and the other receives none.
distractorRationale.b: This is wrong because only the products of the affected secondary cell are abnormal; the other secondary cell (first polar body line) divides normally.
distractorRationale.c: Homologue separation is the meiosis I step. A meiosis II error concerns sister chromatids, not homologues.
distractorRationale.d: Polyploidy (e.g. triploidy) arises from fertilisation by two sperm or a diploid gamete, not from a single non-disjunction event.

questions.explanation: At meiosis II sister chromatids normally separate. If they fail to do so, the secondary oocyte divides into one cell with two copies and one with none of that chromosome; only the descendants of that one cell are abnormal. This differs from meiosis I non-disjunction, where all four products are abnormal.

questions.stem: A child with trisomy 21 is studied with DNA markers. The child carries two different chromosome 21 alleles from the mother (one from each of her two homologues) and one from the father. Which conclusion is most consistent with this finding?

options.text: Non-disjunction of homologues in maternal meiosis I
Non-disjunction of sister chromatids in maternal meiosis II
Non-disjunction in paternal meiosis I
A post-zygotic mitotic error producing mosaicism

questions.correctOptionText: Non-disjunction of homologues in maternal meiosis I

distractorRationale.a: Correct: inheriting both different maternal homologues means the homologues failed to separate at meiosis I.
distractorRationale.b: A meiosis II error delivers two copies of the same homologue (identical apart from recombination), not both different homologues.
distractorRationale.c: The extra chromosome here is maternal, not paternal.
distractorRationale.d: A post-zygotic error would give a mosaic with a normal cell line and would not explain two different maternal homologues in the gamete.

questions.explanation: Two homologues are different copies, one originally from each of the mother's own parents. Both are only present together in the gamete if homologues did not separate in meiosis I; a meiosis II error would give two identical sister chromatid copies. The extra chromosome is of maternal origin, as in the majority of cases.

questions.stem: A 3-day-old term infant is hypotonic, has a flat facial profile, upslanting palpebral fissures and a single palmar crease. An echocardiogram is requested. Which congenital heart lesion is most characteristic of the suspected condition?

options.text: Atrioventricular septal defect
Coarctation of the aorta
Pulmonary valve stenosis alone
Transposition of the great arteries

distractorRationale.a: Correct: AVSD is the typical congenital heart lesion in Down syndrome.
distractorRationale.b: Coarctation is associated with Turner syndrome, not Down syndrome.
distractorRationale.c: Isolated pulmonary stenosis is not the typical lesion; it is associated with other syndromes such as Noonan syndrome.
distractorRationale.d: Transposition is not characteristically linked to trisomy 21.

questions.explanation: The features describe Down syndrome (trisomy 21). Around half of affected infants have congenital heart disease, with atrioventricular septal defect (endocardial cushion defect) the most characteristic. Coarctation of the aorta is the lesson's cardiac link for Turner syndrome instead.

questions.stem: A 15-year-old girl is 135 cm tall, has a webbed neck, a broad chest and has not entered puberty. Pelvic ultrasound shows streak gonads. Which karyotype and nuclear sex chromatin (Barr body) finding fit best?

options.text: 45,X with no Barr body
47,XXY with one Barr body
47,XXX with two Barr bodies
47,XX,+21 with one Barr body

distractorRationale.a: Correct: Turner syndrome is 45,X; with only one X, which stays active, there is no Barr body.
distractorRationale.b: 47,XXY is Klinefelter syndrome, a male phenotype with small testes.
distractorRationale.c: 47,XXX (triple X) females are usually tall and often have few physical features and normal fertility.
distractorRationale.d: Trisomy 21 produces a different phenotype and one Barr body in a female, but would not explain streak gonads.

questions.explanation: Short stature, webbed neck, shield chest and streak gonads with absent puberty define Turner syndrome (45,X). Each cell has only one X, which remains active, so no inactive X (Barr body) is seen; the other options give the wrong sex phenotype or syndrome.

questions.stem: Which explanation best accounts for the rising incidence of trisomy 21 with advancing maternal age?

options.text: Primary oocytes remain arrested in prophase I for decades, during which the structures holding homologues together deteriorate
Older mothers accumulate point mutations in chromosome 21 genes which are transmitted to the fetus
Older mothers produce more oocytes per cycle, increasing the chance that an abnormal one is fertilised
Older mothers have a higher rate of mitotic division errors in the early embryo

questions.correctOptionText: Primary oocytes remain arrested in prophase I for decades, during which the structures holding homologues together deteriorate

distractorRationale.a: Correct: prolonged prophase I arrest leads to loss of cohesion between homologues and mis-segregation.
distractorRationale.b: Trisomy is a change in chromosome number, not a point mutation.
distractorRationale.c: Women ovulate one oocyte per cycle and the pool declines with age; the number of oocytes does not increase.
distractorRationale.d: Post-zygotic mitotic errors cause mosaicism, which is uncommon, and are not the main explanation for the age effect.

questions.explanation: Primary oocytes start meiosis I before birth and arrest in prophase I until ovulation, which may be 40 years later. Over that time cohesion between homologues weakens, so non-disjunction at meiosis I becomes more likely. This is a chromosome-number problem, not a point-mutation problem.

questions.stem: A primary spermatocyte undergoes normal meiosis I. In one of its two secondary spermatocytes the sister chromatids of chromosome 21 fail to separate at meiosis II, whereas the other secondary spermatocyte divides normally. What percentage of the four resulting spermatids carry exactly one copy of chromosome 21? Give your answer as a percentage (%).
questions.explanation: The normal secondary spermatocyte gives two spermatids with one copy of chromosome 21 each. The affected secondary spermatocyte gives one spermatid with two copies and one with none. So 2 of 4 spermatids have exactly one copy, which is 50%.

questions.stem: A regional service quotes the risk of a trisomy 21 pregnancy as 1 in 1250 at maternal age 25 and 1 in 100 at maternal age 40 (illustrative figures). By what factor is the risk at 40 higher than the risk at 25? Give the fold increase as a number (no unit; write 'fold').
questions.explanation: The fold increase is the ratio of the two probabilities: (1/100) divided by (1/1250) equals 1250/100 = 12.5. The risk rises steeply and non-linearly with maternal age.

questions.stem: A 24-year-old tall man with sparse facial hair, gynaecomastia and small firm testes is investigated for infertility. (a) Name the likely karyotype and the mechanism by which it arises. (b) Predict his expected hormonal findings and Barr body count, and explain them.
markingGuide: Arises from non-disjunction in meiosis in either parent (two X chromosomes in the ovum, or X and Y not separating in paternal meiosis I) giving an n+1 gamete.
Seminiferous tubule damage causes small firm testes and azoospermia with low or low-normal testosterone.
Raised FSH and LH due to loss of negative feedback from inhibin and testosterone.
One Barr body, because one X is active and the additional X is inactivated.
Clinical features such as tall stature and gynaecomastia linked to relative androgen deficiency.
questions.explanation: The features indicate Klinefelter syndrome (47,XXY), caused by non-disjunction producing an XX or XY gamete. Testicular failure reduces testosterone and inhibin, so pituitary LH and FSH rise. All but one X chromosome is inactivated, leaving one Barr body.

questions.stem: Explain why the risk of a trisomy 21 pregnancy increases with maternal age, and describe how the gametes would differ if the non-disjunction occurred at meiosis I rather than meiosis II. Why is paternal age not a comparable risk factor?
markingGuide: Primary oocytes form in fetal life and arrest in prophase I until ovulation, possibly for decades.
Prolonged arrest leads to deterioration of cohesion and chiasmata holding homologues together, so homologues mis-segregate.
Meiosis I non-disjunction: homologues fail to separate, so all four products are abnormal (two n+1, two n-1 in spermatogenesis; in oogenesis the ovum is n+1 or n-1).
Meiosis II non-disjunction: sister chromatids fail to separate, so only the two products of one secondary cell are abnormal; the other two are normal.
Sperm are produced continuously from puberty and complete meiosis within weeks, so there is no long prophase I arrest and no comparable age effect on trisomy.
Fertilisation of an n+1 gamete by a normal gamete gives trisomy 21; n-1 gives non-viable monosomy 21.
questions.explanation: The age effect comes from the long prophase I arrest of oocytes with deterioration of the apparatus that holds homologues together. Meiosis I errors affect all four products, meiosis II errors only half, and sperm do not have a similar arrest.

questions.stem: True or false: Most girls with Turner syndrome (45,X) have severe intellectual disability.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: Most women with Turner syndrome have normal general intelligence, although some have specific difficulties such as visuospatial or numerical processing. The main features are short stature, gonadal failure, webbed neck and cardiac or renal anomalies.
